title: New Orleans style compared with the playing in Jacksonville and elsewhere
summary: White says the Louisiana style, with its beat and variations, was unlike anything elsewhere, whereas Jacksonville musicians stuck to the note.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Was the New Orleans style you felt different? Was that the New Orleans influence?

Yes, they had the New Orleans style down there too. Those boys definitely had, they had the stomp and the beat and everything on the New Orleans style. Well, I began to like it so well, till after my winter closed in 1917, I went back down there. Tell me this, say in the east,
around Florida and North Carolina, even further north, had you come across any style like that? Well- Is there a difference in the Louisiana style, say, and the other east?

Very, very different. Very different. There was no style, nowhere in the United States similar to the style of the playing of the fellas around in lower Louisiana and especially New Orleans. They had variations on the theme, whatever the number was. They had such variations on such wide variety of variations, until it would astound you. Yeah, it did me when I first started. Yes, that's just the truth. Now in places like Jacksonville, we had wonderful musicians around Jacksonville, like Tony Jackson and Connie Michael and fellas like that, Willie Lewis, whom I mentioned a while ago. They played, but they played just as near correct as they could. Stuck right to the note. Yeah. Well, you take the Johnson brothers, Dr. Weldon Johnson and James Roseman Johnson, that's their home. Then I had a fellow named Shermie playing cornet with me out of the Edward Waters College there in the Jacksonville concert band. He used to play in one of the ragtime bands around Jacksonville and then Love Lee. And while I'm on the Jacksonville subject here, a wonderful band. Jacksonville had a wonderful band, but it was never stationed in Jacksonville as a Jacksonville's own. Because this fine musician, Eugene Michael, having resigned his position at Tuskegee Institute, he was a sort of a musician on tour always. And he would always come and bring his fine band of musicians off some concert tour to Jacksonville. And he always carried 25 pieces. Michael was a fine director, fine pianist, fine violinist, and a beautiful cornetist. Not nothing exciting, but just a strictly business cornet player. Fine.
